tip_title: If You Work From Home, Your Homeowners Policy Has a Business Blind Spot You Should Know About.
topic: Home-Based Business Insurance - Equipment and Liability Gap
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: If You Work From Home, Your Homeowners Policy Has a Business Blind Spot You Should Know About.**

Standard homeowners and renters policies weren't built with remote work in mind. Most cap coverage for business equipment at somewhere around $2,500, and that cap applies whether your work gear is sitting on your kitchen table or in a bag at the airport. More importantly, if a client, delivery driver, or contractor gets hurt at your home during a business interaction, your homeowners liability coverage may not respond to that claim at all. For a lot of households — especially those with a dedicated home office or a small side business — there's a real gap between what they think is covered and what actually is. The fix is usually an endorsement added to your existing policy, not a separate business policy, and it's often less expensive than people expect.

Not sure if your current policy covers how you actually use your home? Ask your Peachy agent — it's a quick check and the answer matters.

📖 [Learn more from the Insurance Information Institute](https://www.iii.org/article/insuring-your-home-based-business)
summary: Covers the gap in standard homeowners and renters policies for home-based workers, specifically the sub-limit on business equipment (typically around $2,500) and the absence of liability protection for business-related injuries on the property, with an endorsement as the gap-filler.
scoring_notes: All three audiences skew educated, professional, and higher-income — remote work and side businesses are common in these demographics. Prior tip on this subject (May 28) covered the same territory from a general awareness angle; this tip sharpens the focus specifically on the equipment sub-limit dollar figure and the liability-for-business-visitors gap, giving readers a concrete number to react to. Evergreen topic (timeliness 6) but highly relevant for these audiences. Source is iii.org (trusted). No carrier names or premium figures.

tip_title: Fall Is the Right Time to Walk Your Property. Your Insurance Company Is Already Thinking About It.
topic: Home Insurance - Fall Maintenance and Coverage Readiness
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Fall Is the Right Time to Walk Your Property. Your Insurance Company Is Already Thinking About It.**

When hurricane season winds down and fall arrives, insurers are quietly paying attention to property condition. Gutters packed with debris, overhanging branches that didn't come down during a summer storm, HVAC units that haven't been serviced — these aren't just maintenance to-dos, they're the kind of deferred upkeep that can complicate a claim if something goes wrong later. Most homeowners policies exclude damage that results from neglect or poor maintenance, which means a clogged gutter that lets water back up into your roof could turn a covered loss into a denied one. A one-hour property walkthrough in September, before leaves pile up and temperatures drop, is one of the cheapest insurance moves you can make. Fix the small stuff now, and you're not explaining deferred maintenance to an adjuster later.

Not sure what your policy's maintenance-related exclusions actually say? Your Peachy agent can point you to the right section of your policy.

📖 [Learn more from the Insurance Information Institute](https://www.iii.org/article/what-does-homeowners-insurance-cover)
summary: Covers fall property maintenance as a proactive insurance move, specifically how deferred upkeep (gutters, overhanging trees, HVAC) can turn a covered loss into a denied claim under standard homeowners policy exclusions, framed as a September walkthrough action item.
scoring_notes: September is the natural transition point between storm season and fall prep. Prior water damage tips (June 29, August 29) covered sudden-vs-gradual exclusions and roof condition specifically; this tip broadens to a full fall property walkthrough framing covering multiple maintenance categories. High homeownership in East Cobb (78%) and meaningful in Perimeter (55%) and Lewisville Lake (65%). Actionable: walk the property this week. Avoids scare tactics by framing as proactive rather than fear-based.

tip_title: September Means Deer Season Is Starting. Your Auto Policy Has Two Very Different Answers for That.
topic: Auto Insurance - Fall Driving Hazards and Coverage Readiness
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: September Means Deer Season Is Starting. Your Auto Policy Has Two Very Different Answers for That.**

Here's something a lot of drivers don't realize until it's too late: hitting a deer is NOT covered by collision insurance. It falls under comprehensive coverage, which is the part of your policy that handles non-collision events like animals, weather, theft, and falling objects. If you only carry liability (and some drivers do, especially on older paid-off vehicles), you have zero coverage for a deer strike. September through November is when deer are most active near roadways, so this is actually a practical thing to check right now before peak season hits. Pull up your auto policy and look for the word "comprehensive" on your declarations page. If it's not there, it's worth a conversation about whether adding it makes sense for your situation.

Not sure what coverages you're currently carrying? Your Peachy agent can pull up your policy and walk through it with you in about five minutes.

📖 [Learn more from the Insurance Information Institute](https://www.iii.org/article/auto-insurance)
summary: Covers the distinction between collision and comprehensive auto coverage specifically in the context of deer strikes during fall peak season, framed as a September action item to confirm comprehensive coverage is in place before activity spikes.
scoring_notes: September is the start of peak deer season across Georgia and Texas. Both audiences have meaningful vehicle ownership. Prior comprehensive/collision tip (June 29) covered the general distinction; this tip takes a deer-season-specific angle tied to a concrete seasonal hazard. Actionable now: check your declarations page before October. Works for both homeowner and renter segments since it's auto-focused. No carrier names, no specific dollar figures.
